sections.content:
A plot twist is an unexpected revelation or turn of events in your story. There are several types of twists:

- An ally turns out to be the bad guy – 006 in Golden Eye
- The bad guy turns out to be the good guy – Snape in the Harry Potter books
- An important element in the story turns out not to be important at all (red herring) – The butler in the Hounds of Baskerville
- The conflict is resolved, but then it isn’t, or a new one appears – In Only Murders in the Building, the sleuths believe they’ve solved the murder…but did they?
- An unreliable narrator who is purposefully deceiving the reader or is misinformed. – Sixth Sense or Pride and Prejudice
- A character or antagonist arrives (or comes back) and upends the story – Gandolf in the Lord of the Rings

In romance, a twist is usually about revelation, either emotional, relational, or identity-based. It shifts what the characters (and readers) believe is true.

There are two broad categories of twists in romance:

External twists: These involve outside circumstances. Secret identities. Hidden enemies. A fake relationship turning real. A long-lost sibling. A business betrayal. Evil twin.

Internal twists: These involve emotional truth. A misbelief exposed. A hidden vulnerability revealed. A character realizing they’ve been wrong about love, themselves, or the other person.

Both can be powerful. But in romance, internal twists often hit harder. For example, the moment Elizabeth Bennet realizes how wrong she’s been about Mr. Darcy.

sections.title: Where Plot Twists Work Best in Romance Structure

sections.content:
Plot twists aren’t random. They work best when strategically placed. Here are three high-impact spots.

1. The Midpoint Shift

The midpoint is where something changes. Instead of reactions, we begin to see characters take action. In romance, this is often where:

- The fake relationship starts to feel real.
- Enemies become reluctant allies.
- A secret attraction is exposed.
- The hero realizes he’s in deeper than he planned.

This is a great place for a twist because it shifts the trajectory of the relationship and the story.

2. The Black Moment

The black moment is where everything falls apart. Whether this is the angsty breakup or a cozy, reluctantly going their own way again, in this spot of the book, the couple breaks apart. Instead of making the black moment predictable (“He lied, she leaves”), consider adding a layer. Maybe:

- The betrayal was actually protection.
- The heroine already knew the truth.
- The villain manipulated the evidence.
- The hero pushes her away to save her.

3. The Third-Act Reveal

Sometimes the twist is about truth.

- The real reason he left years ago.
- The secret she’s been carrying.
- The true identity of the antagonist.

This reveal should force a character to make a new choice rooted in growth.

sections.title: Six Types of Romance Plot Twists

sections.content:
If you’re looking for inspiration, here are six twist categories that work well in romance:

1. The Secret Identity Twist

- He’s undercover.
- She’s royalty.
- He’s the anonymous texter.
- She’s the mystery author he’s been arguing with online.
- He’s the anonymous man she’s been falling for online (You’ve Got Mail).

Secret identities naturally create tension and emotional payoff. The challenge is to pull it off in a way that doesn’t have the other character feeling completely duped and unable to trust.

2. The Betrayal That Wasn’t

- It looked like cheating.
- It looked like sabotage.
- It looked like he chose someone else.

But the truth reveals something entirely different. I once wrote a story (unpublished) in which the wife of a man had amnesia. He was encouraged by her doctor to let her memory return on its own, rather than push her to remember by telling her their history. As a result, while the husband is helping her, she doesn’t fully understand their relationship, but that doesn’t stop her from falling for him. When she reads in the paper that he’s married, she believes she’s the mistress and gets angry. The scene culminates in his telling her that he is married…to her.

The betrayal lie can also work well in romantic suspense. Sandra Brown often uses this to make readers second-guess the protagonists.

3. The Villain Flip

- The best friend.
- The parent.
- The trusted coworker.
- The charming mentor.

Revealing that someone close has ulterior motives raises the stakes significantly. Of course, the opposite of this happens in Harry Potter (spoiler alert), in which Snape turns out to be a hero.

4. The Sacrificial Lie

- “I don’t love you.”
- “You deserve better.”
- “I never cared.”

Except it’s a lie told to protect. This protection could be physical. For example, a man who has the mafia after him might say this to make the woman he loves leave him. But it could be emotional protection or the result of low self-esteem. For example, he may really feel she deserves better. Or he wants her to pursue her dreams and believes he’ll hold her back.

This trope is powerful when handled carefully. The motivation must be believable.

5. The Escalation Twist

- The threat isn’t random.
- The stalker is closer than expected.
- The danger is connected to the hero’s past.

In romantic suspense, this type of twist heightens both plot and intimacy.

6. The Perspective Shift

We thought he didn’t care. We thought she was cold. We thought he was arrogant. We thought he was alive (The Sixth Sense).

Then we see the truth.

This type of twist works well in dual POV because readers may know something the other character doesn’t until the moment of reveal.

sections.title: How to Write a Twist
use_cases: Use when planting subtle dialogue clues that carry double meanings for later reveals
Implement when elevating an seemingly benign character into a pivotal plot catalyst
Configure when layering subplots to camouflage critical information until the climax
Use when challenging a character's core internal flaw or misbelief to force growth

sections.content:
Plot twists are no easy feat. You don’t just toss them in willy-nilly to shake things up because if readers feel tricked, you’ve failed.

So how do you make sure your twist lands?

Plant Emotional Breadcrumbs

Twists must be set up from the very beginning. In many ways, it’s like plotting a mystery that requires clues and herrings.

Ask: – What subtle line of dialogue could carry double meaning? – What behavior could seem normal but later feel suspicious? – What wound or fear could foreshadow the reveal?

Readers shouldn’t predict the twist, but they should recognize the clues afterward.

Elevate an Inconsequential Character

Take a character that seems benign and turn them into the linchpin or the crucial element of the plot. For example, Samwise in The Lord of the Rings isn’t inconsequential, but as it turns out, he’s the hero, when all along we thought it was Frodo.

Use Misdirection

Elements such as red herrings, sleight of hand, and dead ends “trick” readers into thinking one thing is important when it’s not, or isn’t important when it is. Again, The Sixth Sense movie uses this masterfully.

Use Character Misbeliefs

Romance is driven by internal conflict. If your character believes something deeply flawed, such as “I’m not enough,” “Love never lasts,” or “I always get left,” the twist can challenge that belief. When the truth surfaces, it forces growth.

Use Lies or Withheld Information

This happens a lot in romance. False identity. Fake marriage/relationship. The overheard lie. The lie that’s actually the truth, but not believed. The lie that isn’t corrected (action is based on assumptions). Just be careful, as readers don’t like it when a simple conversation could clear up a misunderstanding.

Layer Subplots

Subplots are excellent camouflage.

That lighthearted friendship? It might be gathering information.

That business deal? It might tie to the antagonist.

That family drama? It might connect directly to the black moment.

Subplots allow you to plant twists without drawing attention.

Avoid Withholding Cheats

One of the fastest ways to lose reader trust is to hide information your POV character knows. If your heroine has known the truth all along, but the reader didn’t because you never showed her thinking about it, that’s not a twist. It feels like cheating. It’s the same as a mystery author withholding the vital clue to solve the murder until the reveal. Readers want all the info so that when the twist comes out, they can rethink what they’ve read and realize they had the clues the whole time.

Going back to the movie The Sixth Sense, when the twist is revealed, the film replays many moments we’ve seen, but now we realize we viewed them incorrectly. That’s what makes this reveal so satisfying.

Make It Matter

If you remove the twist and the story still works the same, it’s not doing enough. A strong twist:

- Raises stakes
- Forces a choice
- Changes the emotional dynamic
- Deepens intimacy or conflict

Here are made-up examples of adding a twist:

Outlander: What if, when Jamie sends Claire back through the stones, he ends up going with her to the future? Now Claire has to choose between Jamie and Frank. Plus, Jamie has to adapt to a 20th-century world.

Jane Eyre: What if, when Jane returns to Thornfield, (spoiler alert) Bertha is still alive?

Red, White, and Royal Blue: What if Prince Henry were a spy for the British government?

I’m not saying these twists would have made these books better. They’re just examples of how you can turn your story on its head with a twist.

sections.title: The Biggest Plot Twist Mistakes in Romance
use_cases: Use when evaluating if a plot twist aligns with romance genre conventions
Implement when structuring the emotional delivery and timing of a revelation
Configure when establishing groundwork to avoid reader dissatisfaction
Use when checking if a narrative pivot serves character development or just shock value
sections.content:
Do you need a crazy plot twist? No. But if you’re going to try it, it mustn’t fall short. Here are mistakes to avoid:

Breaking the HEA contract: No matter how shocking, you cannot twist away the genre promise of a happy ending.

Twisting only for shock: If it doesn’t serve character growth and movement toward the HEA, then it’s not necessary.

Adding it too late: If you introduce a twist in the final chapter without groundwork, readers will feel blindsided. I once read a mystery in which a suspect was introduced right before the murder reveal, and he was the murderer. I felt cheated!

Using coincidence: Twists must feel inevitable in hindsight. Not random.

Ignoring emotional fallout: A twist without reaction is flat. Show the shock. The anger. The heartbreak. The relief. This is the stuff readers are reading for!

sections.title: A Quick Twist Test for Your Work in Progress
use_cases: Use when evaluating the impact of a narrative shift on character relationships
Implement when checking if plot clues sufficiently support a major revelation

sections.content:
If you’re considering adding or strengthening a twist, ask yourself:

- Does this deepen the relationship?
- Does it raise emotional stakes?
- Can readers look back and see the clues?
- Does it force a character to grow?
- Would removing it weaken the story?

If you can answer yes to most of those, you’re on the right track.

The best plot twists in romance don’t change the destination. Instead, they add another element of tension to the story. They take readers from “Of course they’ll end up together” to “Oh my goodness, how are they ever going to fix this?”

sections.title: A hidden plot and a visible plot
use_cases: Use when constructing complex narrative payoffs through dual plot lines
Implement when hiding a true story outcome behind a distracting red herring
Configure when mapping key story moments to support two simultaneous interpretations
Use when designing a twist that must feel more satisfying than the anticipated ending
sections.content:
In this note, we’ll talk about a second, slightly more complex way to deliver a satisfying subversion of expectations. In this approach, you use the setup to establish multiple appropriate realms of outcomes. Like an illusionist’s sleight of hand, you point the audience’s expectation toward a particular outcome, a “red herring” of sorts. Then, in the payoff you deliver a subtler but more meaningful one.

This type of payoff is constructed so that key moments in the story support both the red herring and the true outcome. I think of this roughly like a DNA double helix. On one side is the more visible plot. Connected to key story moments in this plot, like rungs on a ladder, are the moments in the hidden plot. Then, in the payoff, the plots swap positions, and the hidden one comes to the fore.

![A diagram with a double helix where one side is highlighted until the helixes cross and then the other side is highlighted.](https://www.natelistrom.com/assets/img/appropriate-payoffs-2.png)

Key to pulling this off, of course, is that the payoff of the hidden plot must feel more gratifying to the audience than the payoff of the visible plot would have. You must always deliver better than expected.

sections.title: Casablanca: love vs. redemption
use_cases: Use when designing parallel plotlines where one subplot obscures the true resolution
Use when developing a character foil to highlight a protagonist's moral decline or growth
Implement when structuring an 'unexpected reversal' to exceed audience expectations
Configure when a secondary character needs to function as both an obstacle and a goal
Use when layering a redemption arc beneath a primary romance or action genre framework
sections.content:
There’s a masterful example in Curtiz’s 1942 film, Casablanca.

Here’s the setup: Rick Blaine is painted as a disillusioned patriot, someone who is capable of great heroism but has become jaded. Next, Ilsa Lund enters the scene. We learn that Ilsa is the reason Rick is jaded. They were lovers, and she abandoned him without explanation the day he fled the Nazi occupation of Paris. Ilsa is now married to Victor Lazlo, a Czech freedom fighter resisting the Nazi occupation of Europe.

There are two plotlines being established here. Lazlo is the connection between them.

The more obvious plotline — the one that audiences inevitable watch closely and anticipate a resolution for — is the love story between Rick and Ilsa. The writers engineer the story in such a way as to make us desire to see Rick’s jaded heart soften and to see the couple reunite in bliss.

In this plotline, Victor Lazlo is played as an obstacle to the goal, a rival to Rick. He is the “man in the way” keeping Ilsa and Rick apart.

Yet, at the same time, Lazlo illustrates the ideal of the freedom fighter Rick used to be (and could be again). This sets up the plotline of Rick’s redemption story.

While Lazlo’s purity and idealism makes him unrelatable, audiences are led to respect his dedication to the cause. Rick respects it as well, though in his disillusioned state he wouldn’t admit it — perhaps not even to himself. Lazlo is a positive foil for Rick.

In the redemption plotline, Victor Lazlo ends up becoming the goal, a macguffin of sorts. Lazlo is the one who must be saved at all costs. If Lazlo is captured by the Nazis, the hope of the freedom of Europe (and the world, by extension — we pull no punches here) goes with him. For Rick’s character to be redeemed, Lazlo must be saved. A

Through the vehicle of Lazlo, major moments in the story that advance the visible, love plotline simultaneously advance the hidden, redpemption plotline.

As the final payoff draws near, audiences are primed to expect Rick and Ilsa to ride of together in romantic bliss. But that’s a red herring. Because Rick must save Lazlo — and because Lazlo could not be what he is without Ilsa — the traditional resolution of the love plotline would not be completely satisfying.

Instead, there is an unexpected reversal. In the final payoff, the hidden redemption plotline that has been building all along takes over. In spite of his deep love for her, Rick chooses to give Ilsa up. This unexpected self-sacrificial twist not only saves Victor Lazlo, it proves that Rick is still worthy of the cause of freedom. He loses the girl, but he recovers his soul. While we were busy watching the love story, all along it was laying the foundation for something deeper — Rick’s redemption. B

---

sections.title: Mastering Unexpected Twists: A Comprehensive Guide to Literary Surprise
use_cases: Use when drafting fictional narratives to increase reader engagement and emotional investment.
Implement when crafting a mystery or thriller to effectively deploy red herrings and misdirection.
Configure when balancing narrative pacing to either accelerate or decelerate the story flow.
Use when developing characters to reveal hidden identities or sudden motivation shifts.
Configure when structured as a first-person or third-person narrative to control the flow of information.
sections.content:
In the world of storytelling, a well‑placed surprise can turn an ordinary narrative into an unforgettable experience. Whether you’re drafting a novel, crafting a short story, or writing a screenplay, mastering unexpected twists is essential for keeping readers engaged and emotionally invested.

This guide explains why surprise is a powerful narrative tool, how it captivates readers, and what you can do to weave it seamlessly into your work.

The article covers foundational concepts, types of twists, techniques for crafting them, structural considerations, case studies, practical writing steps, common pitfalls, advanced strategies, and concluding insights.

- Surprise is an event or revelation that defies reader expectations.
- Key components: Unpredictability, Impact, and Relevance to the story.

Surprise taps into curiosity, triggers emotional responses, and enhances memory retention. When readers anticipate something and it turns out differently, their brains release dopamine, making the moment memorable.

- Pacing: A twist can accelerate or decelerate narrative flow.
- Tension: It heightens suspense by disrupting expectations.
- Character Development: Reveals hidden motives or new identities.
- Thematic Reinforcement: Subverts or confirms themes in unexpected ways.

- Reversal: A major change in direction or outcome. Example: In The Sixth Sense, the protagonist discovers he is dead.
- Redirection: Shift from one narrative path to another. Example: In Gone Girl, the investigation pivots from a missing wife to an elaborate deception.

- Hidden Identity: Revealing a character’s true nature or background. Example: The villain in The Dark Knight is actually the hero’s former ally.
- Motivation Shift: Unexpected change in a character’s goals or loyalties. Example: In Harry Potter, Draco Malfoy secretly aids Harry during the final battle.

- Subverted Theme: Turning an expected moral into its opposite. Example: The fairy tale“ Beauty and the Beast” flips the idea that beauty is always desirable.

- Non-linear Narrative: Flashbacks or time jumps that alter perception. Example: Cloud Atlas interweaves stories across centuries, revealing connections later.
- Unreliable Narrator: Perspective that misleads the reader. Example: In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden’s narration is filtered through his biases.

Balance subtle hints with misleading clues to build anticipation. In The Girl on the Train, the narrator’s obsession with a couple foreshadows a hidden crime, while red herrings keep readers guessing.

Steer focus toward a false conclusion before revealing truth. Example: In Shutter Island, the protagonist believes he is investigating a missing patient, but the twist reveals he’s part of an experiment.

- End scenes on unresolved tension to heighten impact.
- Example: The final chapter of The Hunger Games ends with Katniss’s decision, leaving readers eager for the outcome.

Optimal moments for twists vary. Early twists set tone; mid‑twists shift direction; late twists deliver payoff. In Breaking Bad, Walter White’s transformation is gradual, culminating in a dramatic final twist.

- First-person can create intimacy and surprise through personal revelations.
- Third-person allows broader perspective, enabling hidden plot twists.
- Example: In The Handmaid’s Tale, the first‑person voice reveals a twist about the protagonist’s past.

Align twists with exposition, rising action, climax, and resolution to maintain coherence. In The Lord of the Rings, Frodo’s betrayal is a mid‑arc twist that propels the story toward its climax.

- Use twists to accelerate narrative flow during tense moments.
- Slow down pacing by revealing subtle surprises early, allowing readers to absorb details.

Leverage secondary threads to amplify surprise effects. In Game of Thrones, the subplot involving Cersei’s secret child adds a twist that impacts the main plot.

- The Sixth Sense: The reveal that Bruce Willis is dead uses foreshadowing, misdirection, and emotional payoff.
- Gone Girl: The twist of Amy’s disappearance being a staged act relies on unreliable narration and red herrings.

Identify foreshadowing cues, misdirection tactics, timing, and emotional payoff to understand why the twist resonates.

- A memorable twist is grounded in character logic and narrative coherence.
- Overused tropes become predictable; originality matters.

Outline the narrative before inserting twists; ensure coherence. Use a storyboard to map where surprises will occur.

- Create multiple versions of key scenes to test surprise impact.
- Example: Draft two endings for a mystery—one with a twist, one without—to compare reader reactions.

Seek reader reactions to gauge effectiveness and adjust accordingly. Use beta readers or writing groups to identify whether the surprise feels genuine.

- Overusing tropes that readers can anticipate.
- Avoid clichés like “the hero’s sacrifice” unless subverted creatively.

Twists that contradict established character traits or plot logic confuse readers. Ensure all twists align with the story’s internal logic.

- Excessive twists can overwhelm and dilute impact.
- Keep surprises focused and purposeful.

Self‑referential twists that comment on storytelling itself. Example: In The End of the World, the narrator reveals they are writing a story about their own life.

- Horror: Twist that turns the victim into the perpetrator.
- Mystery: Twist that reveals the detective is the culprit.
- Romance: Twist that shows love is a misinterpretation of friendship.

In digital narratives, incorporate visual or auditory elements to surprise readers. Example: A web novel reveals hidden text when the reader scrolls past a certain point.

- Surprise is an engine that drives engagement, pacing, and emotional depth.
- Mastering twists requires understanding types, techniques, structure, and psychological impact.
- Practice planning, drafting, revising, and seeking feedback to refine your surprises.

Experiment with different twist styles, test them in varied genres, and let curiosity guide you. The more you practice, the sharper your surprise craft will become.

- Write a short story incorporating at least one unexpected twist.
- Use the checklist above to evaluate its effectiveness.
- Share with peers for feedback and iterate until it feels truly surprising.

sections.title: Why Be Original?
use_cases: Use when planning narrative twists to ensure they serve a strategic purpose
Implement when evaluating if a manuscript aligns with specific genre requirements
Configure when balancing familiar story frameworks with original element delivery
Use when seeking to increase reader engagement and post-reading recommendations
sections.content:
Before we look at how to turn things on their heads, you should understand that it is still necessary for authors to follow or meet reader expectations most of the time—at least for the big, important ones. Structure and certain plot points or beats are essential and provide a familiar framework for readers, allowing them to navigate the story easily.

Certain tropes or parameters are also required for your manuscript to fit within your chosen genre. For example, your cozy mystery with a career detective solving a gruesome crime isn’t subverting expectations. Your manuscript is simply not that subgenre anymore. If you twist something for your reader, you need to do so intentionally and strategically.

When done well, the techniques used to subvert reader expectations can be of great benefit to a novel. When you surprise a reader in a good way, your book sticks in their mind. They’ll recommend it to friends and take the time to leave a review. But a novel that’s too predictable or littered with clichés will soon be forgotten.

To properly mix things up, you need to watch your frequency of employing this writing technique—i.e., is it twist after twist after twist in a few short pages? And you need to ensure you have a purpose for each topsy-turvy moment. Here are a few ways you can work to subvert reader expectations in your book.

sections.title: Blend Genres
use_cases: Use when aiming to elevate a traditional premise through speculative elements
Implement when transitioning between two distinct literary styles smoothly
Configure when designing a plot that requires high narrative unpredictability
Use when building a unique world that incorporates multiple established frameworks
sections.content: Blending genres can show creativity because you are potentially combining elements in a way no one has before or, at least, not many have done before. For example, Philip K. Dick’s The Man in the High Castle starts out as an alternate-history novel until a science-fiction element comes into play. By melding these genres (in a smooth transition that fits the rest of the plot and doesn’t seem random), Philip K. Dick takes something seemingly ordinary yet horrifying (the Axis powers won World War II) and turns it into a speculative story (hallucinatory visits to an alternate universe) that keeps readers wondering what’s next.

sections.title: Switch Character Roles
use_cases: Use when developing complex character backgrounds to avoid clichés
Implement when designing unique personality traits for secondary characters
Configure when drafting plot points that require unexpected character behavior
Use when reviewing a manuscript to ensure characters are three-dimensional
sections.content: The villain lives happily ever after. Instead of a wise old man, a child is the sage or mentor. The love interest turns the protagonist down for good. Like with these examples, try mixing up some minor tropes. Every human being—or fae or werewolf or other species—is unique, and using stereotypes as the basis for descriptions or actions will turn away readers. Be creative when it comes to blending who your characters are with what they say and do. The tough bodyguard who doesn’t put up with any tomfoolery also knits with people in a retirement community.

sections.title: Challenge Clichés
use_cases: Use when drafting narrative content to avoid overused tropes or predictable plot devices
Configure when establishing a unique authorial voice through original descriptions
Implement when revising dialogue to replace common idioms with descriptive language
Use when seeking to subvert genre expectations by turning standard reveals around
sections.content: Two lovers literally bumping into each other. A single tear falling down someone’s cheek. Every chapter beginning with someone waking up. These examples are clichés that are easily avoidable by getting innovative and being conscious of what is and is not overdone. You can challenge clichés, like the “Scooby Doo reveal” where everyone is standing around in a circle as the villain is apprehended, by turning them around. Brainstorm original wording over idioms, such as “the rain hammered down to flood the streets” instead of “it was raining cats and dogs.” Or find other ways to surprise readers.

sections.title: Unreliable Narrators
use_cases: Use when crafting a psychological thriller to keep the reader guessing about the protagonist's motives
Implement when designing a plot twist that requires re-evaluating previously established facts
Configure when seeking to subvert literary tropes and challenge audience expectations
sections.content: Though some people may object to this narrative style as being confusing or even “cheating,” an unreliable narrator leaves room to subvert expectations. In Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl, our initial narrator, Nick, is revealed as unreliable early on when he notes he lied to the police for the fifth time without informing readers what was a lie and what was the truth. We also have diary entries from Amy, whose character is suddenly revealed to be unreliable halfway through the book, and thus her diary entries become suspect. Nick’s unreliable narration makes readers wonder what is true from the beginning. Then Amy’s plot twist makes them see the story and characters in a whole different light.

sections.title: Play with Time
use_cases: Use when building suspense by revealing outcomes before their causes
Implement when managing multiple complex timelines that converge in a finale
Configure when seeking to subvert standard chronological story structures
Use when the mystery of 'how' it happened is more important than 'what' happened
sections.content: When you play with time, you play with the reader’s anticipation. Many books have event A lead to event B, which leads to event C. Showing your reader a hint of event C, then switching to part of A, and then transitioning to the middle of B will keep the reader wanting to know how it all connects. You can reverse or mix up the order of events to slowly reveal the full picture. You can also merge different timelines and even completely different stories—that connect somehow in the end of course. This arrangement subverts reader expectations by breaking from a standard chronological narrative.

sections.title: Challenge Morality
use_cases: Use when developing complex characters that resist simple 'hero' or 'villain' labels
Implement when attempting to foster reader empathy for a primary antagonist
Configure when layering moral dilemmas that force readers to question a character's intentions
Use when subverting traditional narrative tropes regarding good and evil
sections.content: Challenge your readers’ perceptions of moral and ethical expectations by making characters act against their own principles or our modern standards. When a protagonist does something against our moral code, we may end up wondering whether their bad actions can be justified by their good intentions. Or perhaps you layer redeeming qualities on your villain so your readers connect with them and their motivations. This would subvert the expected novel-reading experience where the bad guy is solely the bad guy. It can make readers understand the antagonist has good intentions but is going about it the wrong way.

sections.title: Use New Symbolic Elements
use_cases: Use when challenging traditional literary tropes or common metaphors to create unique atmosphere.
Implement when selecting alternative imagery and allegories that diverge from genre clichés.
Configure when balancing narrative originality with the maintenance of core reader expectations.
Use when evaluating if twists and subversions are effectively integrated or potentially alienating.
sections.content:
Subvert common metaphors or symbols by avoiding them or using them in new ways. For example, rainy and dark days are usually seen as ominous. Perhaps an author writes rain only when there are happy scenes. Choose imagery and allegories that make sense for your story. A cozy mystery set in a bookstore can have a ferret instead of a cat. A fantasy can use magic through ham radios instead of fancy gadgets. Play with symbolism and symbolic elements to make things interesting.

I’m going to repeat myself here: it is still necessary for authors to follow or meet reader expectations most of the time—at least for the big, important ones. If you throw in a last-second twist that leaves the reader feeling duped, they’re not going to pick up your next book. Don’t take your subversions too far where readers see them as farcical or insincere. Do ensure you’re still being original in particular and intended ways.

If you want to know if your twists and turns are enough or too much, contact me today for help. As a comprehensive editor, I can work with you on subverting expectations through a brainstorming call, an outline critique, a manuscript evaluation, or a developmental edit. Let’s keep your readers on their toes by making your work truly original.

sections.title: What is Mystery Reader Misinterpretation?
use_cases: Use when crafting plot twists that maintain narrative integrity
Implement when planting clues that serve dual purposes in a mystery
Configure when balancing the difficulty of a puzzle for target audiences
Use when analyzing reader psychology and satisfaction statistics
Implement when avoiding 'cheating' tropes in investigative fiction
sections.content:
Simply put, mystery reader misinterpretation is when a writer gently guides a reader to the wrong conclusion on purpose. The writer plants clues and information that seem to point to one suspect, one motive, or one solution. The smart reader picks up on these clues and feels clever for solving the puzzle… only to discover they’ve been brilliantly tricked. The real solution was hidden in plain sight all along, but they misinterpreted the evidence.

This is different from “cheating” the reader. The writer must play fair. All the real clues to the true solution must be there, just presented in a way that readers are likely to read them differently. Think of it like an optical illusion for your brain. You see one image, but when you look closer, you see a completely different one.

A survey of mystery readers found that over 82% say a “surprising yet fair” ending is the most important part of a satisfying mystery. We don’t actually want to guess the killer on page one. We want to be led down a garden path, enjoy the scenery, and then have our minds blown when we find out the path led somewhere unexpected. That “Aha!” moment is the joy of the genre.

So, how do writers make us misinterpret what we’re reading? They use specific, time-tested tools. Understanding them makes you a sharper reader and a more cunning writer.

sections.title: 1. The Red Herring: The Classic Misleader
use_cases: Use when designing a mystery plot to distract readers from the true culprit
Implement when a character needs a plausible secondary motivation to explain suspicious behavior
Configure when planting physical evidence intended to implicate the wrong suspect
Use when developing believable narrative subplots that resolve independently of the main conflict
sections.content:
This is the most famous tool. A red herring is a false clue designed to distract and mislead. The name comes from an old trick of using strong-smelling fish to throw hunting dogs off a trail.

Examples in stories:

- A character is seen buying a weapon, but they bought it for a completely innocent reason.
- A secretive character acts guilty because they’re hiding a different, smaller secret (like an affair or a debt), not the murder.
- A piece of evidence (like a monogrammed handkerchief) is planted to point squarely at the wrong person.

The key is that a red herring must be believable. It can’t be a random, weird event. It must fit the story enough to make the reader think, “Of course! It all makes sense!” until the real truth is revealed.

sections.title: 2. Character Misdirection
use_cases: Use when designing subplots to divert the reader's suspicion toward characters with clear motives
Implement when crafting an unreliable narrator to obscure key plot details
Configure when subverting character tropes by making the antagonist appear helpful or vulnerable
Use when addressing credibility gaps in complex mystery writing
sections.content:
Writers play with our expectations about people.

- The Obvious Suspect: The person with a clear motive, like the spouse or the disgruntled business partner. They seem too obvious, so we might rule them out, or they seem just obvious enough to be convincing.
- The Unreliable Narrator: The person telling the story (like in a first-person novel) might be lying, forgetting key details, or seeing things incorrectly. We interpret events through their eyes, and if their vision is cloudy, ours is too. For more on creating believable characters, see our guide on addressing credibility gaps in mystery writing.
- The “Too Nice to Be Guilty” Character: Writers know we often suspect the mean or shady character. So, they make the real villain charming, helpful, or vulnerable, making us unwilling to suspect them.

sections.title: 3. Information Framing
use_cases: Implement when hiding critical information inside action-heavy sequences to prevent immediate detection
Configure when allowing readers to form incorrect logical conclusions based on juxtaposed facts
Use when restricting reader knowledge to a specific character's limited perspective
Implement when building long-term narrative payoffs through subtle foreshadowing
sections.content:
This is a subtle but powerful trick. It’s how and when a clue is presented.

- Hiding Clues in Plain Sight: A vital piece of information is given during a tense, action-packed scene. Readers are so focused on the drama that they gloss over the important detail. Later, they realize they saw it but didn’t observe it.
- The Power of Assumption: The writer lets readers make a logical leap. For example: “He heard a gunshot and ran into the room. Mr. Smith was dead on the floor, a gun in his hand.” Many readers will assume suicide. But the text never says that. It just says the gun was in his hand. Who put it there?
- Selective Point of View: The story only shows us what one character sees and knows. If they don’t have all the information, neither do we. This naturally leads to misinterpretation.

sections.title: 4. Exploiting Reader Psychology
use_cases: Use when designing complex red herrings based on pattern subversion
Implement when introducing characters to leverage cognitive anchoring
Configure when establishing misleading sequences of events
Use when constructing mystery plots that require psychological manipulation of the audience
sections.content:
Great mystery writers know how our brains work.

- We Look for Patterns: If two similar events happen, we assume they’re connected by the same cause. A writer might set up a pattern (a series of thefts) only to reveal the final event in the pattern (a murder) was actually a copycat or an unrelated crime.
- We Trust First Impressions: The first description of a character or the first theory presented by the detective sticks in our mind. Writers use this to anchor our suspicions in the wrong place.

sections.title: For Writers: How to Master Misinterpretation (Without Cheating)
use_cases: Use when structuring a mystery plot to ensure fair play with the reader
Implement when crafting red herrings to distract from the true culprit
Configure when balancing the visibility of true clues versus false leads
Use when utilizing character dialogue to intentionally mislead the audience
Implement when testing narrative pacing and mystery difficulty with beta readers
sections.content:
1. Know the Truth First: Before you write a single red herring, you must know the real solution, culprit, and motive inside and out.
2. Play Fair: Every real clue to the true ending must be present in the story. When the reader looks back, they should be able to see how they were fooled. This builds satisfaction, not anger.
3. Balance the Clues: Weave your false clues (red herrings) and your true clues together. Give equal “screen time” to both. The true clues should be slightly less shiny or pointed, but they must be there.
4. Test Your Mystery: Give your story to a beta reader. Ask them: Who did you suspect and why? When did you guess the ending? If they guess too early, you need more misinterpretation. If they feel cheated or confused, your true clues might be too weak.
5. Use Dialogue to Mislead: Characters can lie, exaggerate, or simply be wrong. Other characters can believe them, sending the reader down a false path. For more on crafting sharp dialogue and plot, check out how to write a mystery short story.

sections.title: For Readers: How to Become a Mystery-Solving Detective
use_cases: Use when analyzing fictional narratives for hidden plot points
Implement when tracking character development and potential misdirection
Configure when documenting chronological events to identify logical gaps
Use when distinguishing between primary evidence and secondary distractions
sections.content:
1. Question Everything: Treat every clue, alibi, and statement with gentle suspicion. Ask yourself: “Could this mean something else?”
2. Take Notes: Jot down clues, timelines, and character motives. Seeing them on paper can help separate solid evidence from emotional reactions.
3. Watch for “Easy Answers”: If the story seems to be pointing very strongly at one person in the first half, it might be a red herring. Ask, “Who benefits from me suspecting this character?”
4. Re-evaluate Characters: Periodically question your assumptions about each character. Has the “nice” one ever been alone at a key moment? Does the “angry” one have a point that everyone is ignoring?
5. Enjoy the Ride: Don’t get so caught up in solving it that you forget to enjoy the atmosphere, the characters, and the suspense. The best misinterpretation makes the journey fun, even when you’re being fooled.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Satisfaction Over Shock
use_cases: Use when designing plot twists to ensure they feel logically earned
Implement when auditing early story events for re-contextualization potential
Configure when balancing surprise with emotional character growth
Use when drafting short form mystery riddles to maintain consistency
sections.content:
The goal of mystery reader misinterpretation is not just a “gotcha” twist. The goal is a satisfying resolution. The ending should:

- Surprise the reader.
- Make Sense logically when explained.
- Re-contextualize the story so that earlier events feel new and different upon a second look.
- Resonate emotionally. The best twists aren’t just clever; they deepen our understanding of the characters and themes, such as exploring how lies destroy family bonds.

Whether you’re weaving a complex novel or penning short mystery riddles, the principles of clever misdirection are the same.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
use_cases: Use when distinguishing between unintentional storytelling errors and intentional reader misdirection
Implement when using red herrings to construct a foundational plot twist
Configure when adapting mystery mechanics for thriller or horror genres
Use when establishing a 'fair play' narrative to ensure reader satisfaction
Configure when practicing scene-level misdirection through multiple interpretative rewrites
sections.content:
Q: Is mystery reader misinterpretation the same as a plot hole?A: No! A plot hole is an inconsistency or a logical error that breaks the story’s rules. Misinterpretation is a planned, logical trail of clues that leads to a wrong but reasonable conclusion. One is a mistake; the other is masterful craftsmanship.

Q: What’s the difference between a Red Herring and a Plot Twist?A: A red herring is a single tool used to create misinterpretation (a false clue). A plot twist is the overall result—the moment of revelation when the misinterpretation is cleared up and the true story is revealed. Red herrings help build the twist.

Q: Can I use these tricks in other genres, like thrillers?A: Absolutely! While crucial in mysteries, these tools are used in thrillers, horror, and even drama. However, the focus may differ. In a mystery vs. a thriller, the mystery is about solving a past puzzle, while a thriller is about stopping a future threat. Misdirection works in both!

Q: How do I avoid making my reader feel tricked or annoyed?A: Play fair. The number one rule is that all genuine clues must be in the text. The reader should feel outsmarted by the culprit and the writer’s cleverness, not feel like vital information was hidden from them unfairly.

Q: Where can I find ideas to practice this?A: Start small! Try writing a short scene where a character finds a broken necklace. First, write it so it seems like evidence of a theft. Then, rewrite the exact same scene so the broken necklace clues the reader in to a secret reunion. Practicing with mystery story ideas for kids or ideas for grade 8 can be a great, low-pressure way to hone your skills.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Dance Between Reader and Writer
use_cases: Use when designing plot twists or subverting reader expectations
Implement when crafting red herrings to lead readers towards false conclusions
Configure when balancing the tension between clues and narrative feints
Use when analyzing the psychological relationship between author and audience
sections.content:
Mystery reader misinterpretation is a delightful dance between the writer and the reader. The writer leads with clever steps and feints (the red herrings, the framed clues). The reader follows, trying to anticipate the next move. The joy is in the momentum, the music, and the final, breathtaking spin that lands in a surprising yet perfect place.By understanding this core mechanic, you deepen your appreciation for every mystery you read and sharpen your skills for every story you write. It’s all about learning to keep the mystery alive from the first page to the last. So, pick up a mystery novel or start writing one. Look for the misinterpretation. Savor it. And then, go out and create some of your own.

Jeanne Riedel is a mother, grandmother, and mystery author who enjoys baking, traveling, and spending time with loved ones. Now retired, she finds joy in writing and believes it’s never too late to follow your dreams. Visit my Social Media Facebook

sections.title: The Fair Play Principle
use_cases: Use when establishing narrative trust between the writer and the audience
Implement when structuring plot twists to ensure they logicially resolve from existing information
Configure when balancing the difficulty of a mystery puzzle to avoid being perceived as unfair
Use when designing clues that hide in plain sight through narrative misdirection
sections.content:
Every great mystery twist rests on the foundation of fair play-the implicit contract between writer and reader that all necessary information will be provided for solving the puzzle. This doesn't mean making things easy; it means playing honestly.

The Golden Rule: Readers should have access to every piece of information needed to solve the mystery, even if they don't recognize its significance until the revelation. The twist should feel like a surprise that makes perfect sense in hindsight.

Consider Agatha Christie's "And Then There Were None." The solution seems impossible until revealed, yet every clue needed to solve it appears in the text. Christie doesn't withhold information; she presents it in ways that misdirect without lying.

sections.title: The Identity Twist
use_cases: Implement when designing a character who aids an investigation while secretly sabotaging it
Use when masking a crime's true motive by presenting a plausible but false financial incentive
Configure when staging a crime scene to create a false alibi through temporal displacement
Implement when writing character dialogue that must be truthful but misleading to the reader
Use when employing psychological heuristics to guide readers toward a specific red herring
sections.content:
The killer turns out to be someone unexpected-but not someone random. This works best when the character has been present throughout the story but disguised their true nature or significance.

Example: The helpful witness who's actually the killer, carefully directing suspicion away from themselves while appearing to aid the investigation. Their helpfulness isn't fabricated behavior-it's genuine assistance with the hidden agenda of controlling the investigation.

Key to Success: The character must have legitimate reasons for being present and involved that don't depend on their guilt. Their innocent persona should be sustainable and believable, not a thin disguise.

The killer is who readers suspected, but their motive is completely different from what everyone assumed. This works because readers focus so heavily on identifying the perpetrator that they don't question why the crime occurred.

Example: The victim's business partner killed them, but not for financial gain as everyone assumes. Instead, they discovered the victim was planning to expose their affair with the partner's spouse, and they killed to prevent their marriage from being destroyed.

Everyone knows who died and roughly when, but the actual cause or timing of death is dramatically different from what it appears. This often involves making an accident look like murder, or vice versa.

Example: The victim appears to have been murdered in their locked study, but they actually died hours earlier in a different location. The killer moved the body and staged the scene to create an alibi for the actual time of death.

Characters who seem unconnected turn out to have hidden relationships that completely reframe the crime. This works best when the hidden relationship explains previously confusing behavior or evidence.

Example: Two suspects who claimed never to have met before the murder are revealed to be siblings separated in childhood, with the crime stemming from a decades-old family secret.

The mark of a masterful twist is that it enhances the story on subsequent readings. Scenes take on new meanings, seemingly innocent dialogue reveals hidden depths, and character motivations become clearer rather than more confusing.

Characters should speak in ways that are truthful from their perspective but can be interpreted differently by readers. This isn't about being deliberately obscure-it's about using the natural ambiguity of language.

Example: A character says, "I never wanted this to happen." On first reading, it seems like general regret about the murder. After the twist reveals they're the killer, it becomes a confession of reluctance-they committed murder but didn't want to.

Include details that support the false conclusion while also supporting the true one. The key is making the false interpretation more obvious initially.

Example: The killer nervously fidgets with their wedding ring during questioning. Initially, this suggests they're lying about their relationship with the victim. Actually, they're nervous because they're about to frame their spouse for the murder.

Present crucial information as if it's unimportant background detail. Readers will note it but not assign it proper significance until the revelation recontextualizes everything.

Example: Casually mention that a character has a key to the victim's house because they water the plants when the victim travels. This seems like innocent background until revealed that this access enabled the murder.

Understanding how readers process information helps you craft more effective twists. Readers naturally form theories and then look for evidence to support them. You can use this tendency to guide them toward false conclusions.

Once readers form a theory about the killer's identity, they'll unconsciously emphasize evidence that supports their theory while downplaying contradictory information. You can exploit this by providing just enough evidence to support a false theory early in the story.

Readers assign greater importance to information that's easily recalled or recently presented. Place your misdirection clues in memorable scenes or repeat them occasionally to keep them prominent in readers' minds.

Readers look for patterns and assume they'll continue. Establish a pattern early (perhaps with red herrings), then break it with your twist. The unexpected deviation creates surprise while the established pattern provides the foundation for fairness.

Twists that require characters to have impossible knowledge or abilities. If your twist depends on a character being in two places at once or knowing something they couldn't possibly have learned, it violates fair play.

Revelations that shock but don't enhance the story. The twist should deepen character development, explain puzzling behavior, or resolve plot threads-not just surprise for surprise's sake.

Twists that work only because crucial information was deliberately hidden from readers. This includes secret meetings that aren't shown, important conversations that happen off-page, or character relationships that are never hinted at.

Reveals that completely contradict established character traits without explanation. If your mild-mannered librarian turns out to be a ruthless killer, there must be psychological foundation for this capacity, even if it was hidden.

Layer multiple revelations so that solving one mystery reveals another. This works best when each twist recontextualizes the previous one rather than simply adding new information.

Events happened in a different order than initially presented. This requires careful handling to avoid confusing readers, but when done well, it can create powerful revelations about causation and motivation.

Reveal that events were viewed from the wrong perspective or that the narrator's understanding was fundamentally flawed. This works best with limited third-person narration following a character who misinterprets events.

sections.title: Testing Your Twist
use_cases: Use when evaluating if a narrative revelation is logically sound and foreshadowed
Configure when performing an audit of clues to ensure fair play for readers
Implement when checking if character motivations remain consistent post-revelation
Use when validating if a plot twist improves the overall satisfaction of the story retrospectively
sections.content:
Before finalizing your plot twist, subject it to rigorous testing:

The Hindsight Test: Does the twist make the entire story more satisfying when viewed in retrospect? Do previously confusing elements now make sense?

The Clue Audit: Can readers find all necessary information in the text before the revelation? Mark every clue that supports your twist and ensure they're all present and accessible.

The Motivation Check: Does the twist provide adequate motivation for all character actions? Can you trace each character's behavior back to logical psychological foundations?

The Fair Play Review: Could a careful, intelligent reader solve the mystery based on the information provided? The answer should be "yes, but it would be difficult."

sections.title: The Emotional Payoff
use_cases: Use when evaluating the resonance of a plot twist beyond basic logic
Implement when seeking to recontextualize character relationships through sudden plot shifts
Configure when balancing intellectual puzzle elements with emotional character development
Use when drafting a climax that requires long-term reader engagement and memorability
sections.content:
The best twists aren't just intellectual puzzles-they're emotional revelations that deepen readers' connection to your characters and story. When crafting your twist, consider not just the logical surprise but the emotional impact.

Ask yourself: How does this revelation change readers' understanding of the characters involved? Does it evoke sympathy, horror, sadness, or understanding? The most memorable twists engage both mind and heart.

A perfect example is the ending of "The Sixth Sense"-the twist completely recontextualizes every previous scene while delivering profound emotional impact about connection, communication, and letting go.

sections.title: Crafting Your Revelation Scene
use_cases: Use when structuring the climax of a mystery novel to ensure organic flow
Implement when transitioning from building suspense to providing resolution
Configure when balancing physical evidence against character dialogue for story reveals
Use when refocusing the story's theme through the lens of a major plot twist
sections.content:
The moment of revelation deserves as much attention as the twist itself. This scene should feel like the natural culmination of everything that came before, not an arbitrary stopping point where information is dumped on readers.

Structure the revelation progressively: Start with hints that something isn't as it seemed, build to the moment of realization, then provide the explanation that ties everything together. Let readers experience the dawning understanding alongside your detective.

Show, don't just tell: Whenever possible, let readers witness proof of the twist rather than just hearing about it. Physical evidence, revealed documents, or confrontations that force confessions are more satisfying than lengthy explanations.

Remember, the plot twist is not the end of your story-it's the key that unlocks the story's true meaning. When done masterfully, it transforms every previous scene, making readers eager to experience your carefully crafted deception all over again. That's the mark of a truly great mystery: one that's even better the second time around.

sections.title: To Reveal or Not Reveal that is the Villainous Question
use_cases: Use when deciding whether to reveal the villain's identity at the start of a manuscript or at the climax
Implement when developing Goal, Motivation, and Conflict (GMC) for antagonistic characters to avoid stereotypes
Configure when balancing the number of secondary characters to keep readers guessing without causing confusion
Use when layering buried clues and red herrings throughout the narrative structure
Apply when writing villain point-of-view scenes to increase reader engagement and explain complex motivations
sections.content:
In a story that braids love and suspense, sensuality and danger, good and evil, life and death you might very well have a triangle of characters. Although many will argue that there is ALWAYS an ‘antagonist’ in every story, that character in a suspense is generally the villain. And in a romantic suspense, the villain not only threatens the lives of the antagonists, he or she represents a threat to their love, as well. So that overcoming the villain is doubly satisfying and creating the villain is complicated and challenging and, as most romantic suspense writers will tell you, really fun.

When you start a romantic suspense, you have to make one all-important decision: to reveal the identity of the villain or not. This choice does have a significant impact on the story ‘ and both routes are correct. There are GREAT suspense stories where you know from page one exactly who the bad guy is, and you’re still on the edge of your seat watching your hero and heroine figure it out or fight him to the death. There are also GREAT suspense stories where you are handed a cast of characters and while you are reading, given clues (and fake clues ‘ called ‘red herrings’ and someone out there is going to tell us why) to figure it out. This is a different kind of game, and a wholly different kind of writing challenge. I call it ‘who knows what’ and the reader is as important in that list as the characters. Some people believe that it’s a ‘mystery’ if the reader solves the crime/identity of villain along with the characters, and a suspense if the reader knows but experiences the characters finding it out. I’m not entirely sure I buy that. I do know this: when I start a romantic suspense, I make a conscious decision to reveal or not reveal the villain and that decision has a profound impact on the book. I lean toward NOT revealing, just because I like to read those books. Either way, my publisher considers it a suspense.

Whether or not you reveal the villain to the reader (or the characters), you have to give your bad guy/girl just as much GMC (goal, motivation and conflict) as your good guy and girl. Meaning, the villain can’t be bad just for the pure joy of being bwa-ha-ha-ha moustache-twirling dastardly. Something has caused that evil soul to hatch — or something has caused a perfectly nice person to do something very bad ‘ and you really should have a pretty good idea what it is before you start. The villain’s goal needs to be clear and believable ‘ but if you are writing the type of suspense where you have chosen NOT to reveal the villain until the end, the villain’s goals cannot be SO clear as to make him/her the obvious choice because the reader will feel cheated. (I told you this was hard.) When you have a group of villains (a terrorist cell, for example) you will probably have to choose one or two to embody the evil.

So when you sit down to do your character charts, map out your GMC and decide the course of your hero and heroine’s backstory, if you are writing romantic suspense, you’ll have to do the same thing for the villain. And you should do this for the people who pepper the plot who are not the villain, but might be. There should be enough of them to keep a reader guessing, but not so many that you’ve created a world of confusion. And, as I’m sure you’ve heard in every lecture on romantic suspense, don’t drop the villain in for the first time in the end of the book. He/she should be there from the beginning. My test: when you finish a book where the villain is not revealed until the end, you should be able to go back to the VERY BEGINNING (if not page one, then pretty darn early) and see the first clue to the true identity of the villain. And the clues should be there (buried, buried, but evident) all through the book.

If you have a villain who is revealed from the beginning, I urge you to consider scenes in his/her point of view. This really helps a reader ‘connect’ with the villain and understand his or her motivation. Plus, it’s just so much fun to let yourself be that bad!

sections.title: Don’t Forget the Love Story
use_cases: Implement when developing the hero and heroine's extraordinary skill sets to foil the villain
Use when justifying high-risk character actions through stakes or backstory motivation
Configure when balancing the suspense plot with the romantic and sensual character arcs
Use when accelerating character relationships within condensed story timelines
Configure when creating high-tension situations that force early intimacy between protagonists
sections.content:
I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention a few words about our hero and heroine. The hero and heroine of a romantic suspense are no different than the h/h in any other romance. All the same qualities are important plus, it helps if they have one or two tricks up their sleeve that make them extraordinary. Rhonda Pollero, who writes for Intrigue as Kelsey Roberts, calls this the character’s ‘superpowers.’ The character needs to be able to do one thing better than the average Joe, and you should be sure the reader knows it so that when you hero pulls his superpower from his bag of tricks to foil the villain, it’s not a surprise to the reader. Whether it’s the heroine’s computer hacking skills, the hero’s night vision, or their ability to interrogate someone without them knowing it give your good guys an ber power that will take them out of the ordinary and into the heroic.

For some reason, the TSTL heroine has a permanent home in romantic suspense. (Too Stupid To Live.) How often have you heard the TSTL heroine described as the one who goes to the pitch black basement, unarmed, in the middle of the night, when there is a murderer on the loose and she heard a noise suspiciously like a knife being sharpened? Because the heroine in romantic suspense has to face life threatening danger, she has to be a risk-taker. Not necessarily by nature but in the course of the story, at some point, she has to take at least one risk, usually more. The way to avoid a TSTL heroine in this case is through MOTIVATION. If her actions are believably set up and motivated, either by the possible consequences if she doesn’t act (ie. her child will die) or by the backstory you’ve set up for her (ie. this is exactly how her twin sister died), then the reader will go along with her taking risks that we, mere mortal women, would not take.

Although the breakneck plot, the life-threatening danger and edge-of-your-seat suspense are critical to the subgenre, the art of characterization will speak to the most important component of all: romance, sensuality and sexual tension. Remember, they’re running to or from danger, but they are also running to or from love. And the outcome of the dangerous situation WILL impact the outcome of their love. Because of the impending danger, many romantic suspense stories will take place in just a few days or weeks. This is a REAL challenge ‘ to craft a believable romance arc that takes them from enemies to friends to lovers to life partners in ten days. Yet, it is done exquisitely well by many authors. There are a number of ways to speed up the falling in love process in a romantic suspense:

They may give into the sexual desire early (or earlier) in the relationship because of the danger of dying

Force the hero and heroine to be in close proximity (even in the same bed) in order to stay alive

Put them in situations where one character can observe the other character’s ‘superpowers’ to accelerate the falling in love process

Create a history between them as former lovers

Intensify their reactions to each other bordering on love/lust at first sight – no time for the slow build

use_cases: Use when identifying potential publishing houses for romantic suspense manuscripts

sections.content:
Trust me, I’ve been out there trying to break in, trying to sell a single title romantic suspense to a mainstream publisher, and I know what exactly what frustration, rejection, disappointment, envy, self-doubt and misery feels like. I also know that persistence and tenacity are every bit as important as talent in this business. And you know it’s true. You have to have thick skin, patience, good friends, wine and chocolate ‘ sometimes daily ‘ to endure what it takes to sell a book.

Yes, publishers are looking for romantic suspense in all of its iterations. You can target a single title house like Pocket (my publisher), Berkley, Ballentine, Bantam, Kensignton, Medallion, NAL, Zebra I’ve probably missed one or two because I did that list from memory. The fact is, there aren’t many. You have more options if you’ll consider epublishing. And Harlequin/Silhouette publishes the Intrigue and Intimate Moments line, both considered category romantic suspense. (Although you should check the guidelines for specifics.) And you should take the time to find out who edits your favorite authors, or who represents them, because they should be at the top of your submission lists.

There are certainly ways to shorten the road to publication, including:

An unpubbed writer is probably not going to sell on proposal. Although, it happens. But rarely. Write the best damn book you’ve got in you and polish it until it shines to a blinding finish. When you complete it, stock up on tenacity, confidence, a couple extra layers of skin and supportive friends and family. You’re going to need them all.

sections.title: Abstract
use_cases: Use when analyzing the difference between presentation order and event order in non-linear narratives

sections.content:
Chris Ware’s Building Stories (2012) is a box containing fourteen items that can be read in any order, and for this reason it appears to offer its readers a great deal of choice over the narrative structure of the work. This paper contrasts Building Stories with the video games Fallout: New Vegas and The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim to demonstrate that although Building Stories does offer choices, these choices are not ultimately meaningful because while the reader can decide the order of presentation, they cannot decide the order of events as they can in the games, and in other examples such as Marc Saporta’s novel Composition No.1. The article draws upon the work of Seymour Chatman, Gonzalo Fresca and Espen Aarseth in analysing narratives in games and texts, and concludes by considering the implications of choice in narrative.

sections.content: Dr Simon Grennan is Leading Research Fellow at the University of Chester and a scholar of visual narrative (www.simongrennan.com). He is author of A Theory of Narrative Drawing (Palgrave Macmillan 2017), co-editor, with Laurence Grove, of Transforming Anthony Trollope: ‘Dispossession’, Victorianism and 19th century word and image (Leuven University Press 2015) and contributor to Representing Multiculturalism in Comics and Graphic Novels. (Routledge 2015) and others. He is the creator of Dispossession, a graphic adaptation of a novel by Anthony Trollope (Jonathan Cape and Les Impressions Nouvelles 2015) and, since 1990, half of international artists team Grennan & Sperandio, producer of over forty comics and books (www.kartoonkings.com). Dr Grennan is Principal Investigator for the two-year research project Marie Duval presents Ally Sloper: the female cartoonist and popular theatre in London 1869-85, funded by an AHRC Research Grant: Early Career (2014).

sections.content: Dr Ian Hague is a Senior Lecturer and Year 3 Coordinator in Contextual and Theoretical Studies at London College of Communication (UAL), where he is based in the Interaction Design and Visual Communication Programme. His research looks at comics and graphic novels, and how they engage with questions of materiality and experience. Ian is the author of Comics and the Senses: A Multisensory Approach to Comics and Graphic Novels (Routledge 2014) as well as numerous shorter pieces, and the co-editor of Representing Multiculturalism in Comics and Graphic Novels (Routledge 2015), Contexts of Violence in Comics (Routledge 2019) and Representing Acts of Violence in Comics (Routledge 2019). In 2009, Ian founded Comics Forum, an annual conference on comics that runs as part of the Thought Bubble sequential art festival in Leeds. In 2011, he launched Comics Forum website, which publishes scholarship from a wide range of academics and thinkers on comics from around the world. Ian is also an experienced designer.

# Conjuring Images when Writing for Comics, Prose, and the Screen

April 22, 2025

by Jessica Maison

![Series banner for The Comics Panel with Comics Committee logo](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/The-Comics-Panel.png)

A writer conjures images for their readers, whether writing prose, film, or comics. Comics writing has a set of best practices that share similarities and differences with screenwriting and prose writing. Most successful stories told in any medium must establish a dynamic world and protagonist while presenting an enticing inciting incident, climax, and resolution. They must create compelling characters with relatable strengths and weaknesses driven by interesting motivations. However, distinct differences exist between these mediums. Writing for comics is a visual medium, as is screenwriting, whereas prose is a language-based medium. Yet all three need to conjure images and dynamically travel through space and time. The way a writer in each medium achieves those feats is where the nuances in the writing techniques exist.

Similar to screenwriting, most of the words a comics writer puts into a script are meant for the writer’s collaborators. The comics writer is creating a world for their editor, penciler, inker, colorist, and letterer. Indirectly, the reader will see a visual interpretation of the writer’s words by that team as illustrated in panels. Directly, the reader will experience the writer’s words in the captions and word balloons, mostly as dialogue. Because comics is a visual medium, the less dialogue the better is a good rule. In a visual medium, the story should be told primarily through images. The writer must decide what images are shown and what ones are not, and there is great complexity in those choices, especially in comics, where such limited space exists to develop the story. If done well, the team of artists will build a compelling world and characters using the writer’s well-crafted blueprint.

Screenwriters use scenes to break up their story, choosing when to cut in and out of scenes and manipulating time to create the flow for their story. In film, each frame is projected on the same space. In comics, each panel (frame) occupies its own space. The writer determines what is shown in those panels, creating an illusion of motion or suspense. Even the page turn plays a significant role in the comic’s pacing. A comics writer must consider what action will be on a spread and what will turn the page. Comics rely on readers to fill in the blanks to make their series of images feel fluid and exciting. The comics writer must guide how the reader fills in those blanks by what they show in the panels and when they show it. A writer and artist create a kind of magic when determining the number of panels to use, what images to put in those panels, and how to place them on the page.

![Page from Ambitious Failures, Richard Fairgray's graphic memoir.](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Fairgray_Memoir_about-panels-scaled-1.jpg)

Page from Ambitious Failures, Richard Fairgray’s graphic memoir.

Alternately, prose writers use only words, relying on their readers’ imagination to transform those words into images. The prose writer can do this with as many words or as few as they desire. They usually spend more time describing the setting, characters, and actions because they do not have a camera or an illustrator to create those images. The prose writer must use the reader’s imagination as the conduit to create visuals.

![Pages from Mary Shelley's School for Monsters: The Killing Stone written by Jessica Maison and illustrated by Anna Wieszczyk.](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Fight-scene-from-Mary-Shelleys-School-for-Monsters_-The-Killing-Stone--1024x778.png)

Pages from Mary Shelley’s School for Monsters: The Killing Stone, written by Jessica Maison and illustrated by Anna Wieszczyk.

A fight scene demonstrates the differences in the three mediums very well. In prose, expressing the character’s internal struggle is just as important as describing the external action in a fight. In film, the writer focuses on what actions the director, designers, and actors need to focus on to advance character and plot. The screenwriter must reveal the character’s internal struggle with key moments in the action or pieces of dialogue to develop the story further. Both in film and prose, much of the action can be shown or described. For a comic writer, there is limited space and no actual motion. The writer can’t show the whole fight scene. They must plan out frames and create movement through the actions they choose to reveal.

![Page from the GLAAD Award winning graphic novel Four Color Heroes by Richard Fairgray, published by Fanbase Press.](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Four-Color-Heroes-670x1024.jpg)

Page from the GLAAD Award-winning graphic novel Four Color Heroes by Richard Fairgray, published by Fanbase Press.

Additionally, a prose writer has more freedom to capture the abstract and invisible than a comics writer. They can take as much time as they want describing these things. In comics, a writer must show a character’s internal struggles using visual images and dialogue. Every emotion or motivation must be revealed in limited space and time. They can use thought balloons but sparingly. It is stronger to convey a character’s thoughts through action. That rule is valid in all mediums but is most crucial in comics.

The way the reader experiences time is different in comics than in novels and in films. A reader processes a comic in many parts all at once. They can see what is happening on the next page, catch glimpses of several dialogue balloons ahead, and continue to see the panels they just read. They aren’t just reading in the present like a novel reader, but also in the near present and recent past. The writer needs to keep that in mind when planning out each page and then each panel. A reader takes in more images at once than it does sentences, and that truth differentiates the approach for a comics writer from a prose writer and even a screenwriter. The way the comics reader experiences space and time is a constraint that, when utilized properly, advances a story in a way that can’t be accomplished in other mediums.

![Page from The Ex-Wives of Frankenstein, written and drawn by Richard Fairgray.](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Ex-Wives-Faigray-scaled-1.jpg)

Page from The Ex-Wives of Frankenstein, written and drawn by Richard Fairgray.

Constraints of each medium are also tools. Comics writers must make their medium’s constraints work for them, just like a screenwriter or novelist. Unlike prose, budget and page count constraints play a significant role in comics and screenwriting. If the budget is small, a comics writer will have to develop more story with less art, and a screenwriter will have to replace higher budget scenes with more contained ones. The prose writer typically doesn’t have to make more with less.

Conjuring images and manipulating space and time is at the core of writing, and the techniques a writer utilizes for a medium are determined by that medium’s relationship to images, space, and time. Keeping those relationships in mind when switching from writing one medium to another will set a writer up for a successful transition.

Explore more articles from THE COMICS PANEL

---

![Author photo: Jessica Maison](https://www.sfwa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/jess-bg-150x150.jpg)

Jessica Maison is a sci-fi, fantasy, and horror author, screenwriter, and comic creator. Plastic Girl is her coming-of-age ecopunk YA novel series set in a climate apocalypse. She is the writer of the award-winning graphic novel series Mary Shelley’s School for Monsters, and her short comics have been featured in anthologies such as Cthulhu is Hard to Spell and Nightmare Theater. She is an IBPA Benjamin Franklin Gold Award winner and Foreword INDIES Award nominee. Her sci-fi speculative short stories have been published by Terraform, and she is the founder of Wicked Tree Press.

Jan-Noël Thon's transmedial approach in Transmedial Narratology and Contemporary Media Culture (2016) provides a synergistic analysis of how narration in films, comic books, and video games works. Focusing on the three aspects of storyworld, narrator, and subjectivity, it sheds light on the forms and functions of these elements and their representations in contemporary texts. It thus also facilitates the comparison and transmedial application of many narratological theories.
